Plantago lanceolata: Grassland, roadsides etc, a common weed of lawns and cultivated ground, on neutral and basic soils.
Plantago major: A common garden weed, particularly in lawns. Rarely in grassy places.
Populus nigra: Moist ground in woods and by streams.
Primula veris: Grassy places, fields and woods with calcareous soils.
Prunella vulgaris: Waste ground, grassland, woodland edges etc, usually on basic and neutral soils.
Prunus mahaleb: Dry hillsides, thickets and open woods.
Punica granatum: Dry limestone soils to 2700 metres in the Himalayas.
Quercus robur: Often the dominant woodland tree, especially on clay soils and in the eastern half of Britain, but avoiding acid peat and shallow limestone soils.
Rhamnus cathartica: Fen peat, scrub, hedges, ash and oak woods, on calcareous often dry soils.
Rheum palmatum: Scrub and rocky places and by streams, 2500 - 4000 metres. Slopes and valleys at elevations of 1500 - 4400 metres in western and northern China.
Rhodiola rosea: Crevices of mountain rocks and on sea cliffs.
Rhododendron simsii: Rocks in ravines, C. and S. Japan.
Ribes nigrum: Hedges and woodlands, often by streams.
Rosa canina: Hedges, scrub, woods, roadsides, banks etc.
Rosmarinus officinalis: Dry scrub and rocky places, especially near the sea.
Rubus fruticosus: A very common and adaptable plant, found in hedgerows, woodland, meadows, waste ground etc.
Rubus idaeus: Moist neglected land, hedgerows and woodland edges.
Rumex acetosa: Meadows, by streams and in open places in woodland. Often found as a weed of acid soils.
Rumex crispus: Growing almost anywhere, it is found especially in grassy places, waste ground, roadsides and near sand dunes and is a serious weed of agriculture.
Salix alba: By streams and rivers, marshes, woods and wet fens on richer soils.
Salvia officinalis: Dry banks and stony places, usually in limestone areas and often where there is very little soil.
Salvia rosmarinus: Dry scrub and rocky places, especially near the sea.
Salvia sclarea: Rocky igneous slopes, mixed deciduous and coniferous woodland, shale banks and roadsides to 2000 metres in Turkey.
Sambucus nigra: Hedgerows, scrub, woods, roadsides, waste places etc, especially on disturbed base-rich and nitrogen rich soils.
Sansevieria trifasciata: A weed of roadsides, abandoned gardens, waste areas, disturbed sites, coastal environs, open woodlands, riparian vegetation and the margins of closed forests in tropical, sub-tropical and warmer temperate regions.
Satureja hortensis: Dry gravelly and stony slopes to 1500 metres.
Satureja montana: Old walls, dry banks and rocks on hillsides, usually on calcareous soils.
Schisandra chinensis: Mixed forests, especially on the margins, also by streams and brooks, usually on sandy soils.
Scutellaria lateriflora: Alluvial thickets, meadows and swampy woods.
Silybum marianum: Waste places, usually close to the sea, especially if the ground is dry and rocky.
Solidago virgaurea: Dry woods, grassland, rocks, cliffs, hedgebanks, dunes etc on acid or calcareous soils.
Stellaria media: Growing almost anywhere, it is a common garden weed.
Syzygium aromaticum: Maritime forests in deep, well-drained sandy, acid loams with a pH as low as 4.5.
Tanacetum parthenium: Mountain scrub, rocky slopes, walls, waste places and a weed of gardens, avoiding acid soils.
Tanacetum vulgare: A common plant of waste ground, hedgerows etc.
Taraxacum officinale: A very common weed of grassland and cultivated ground.
Terminalia bellirica: Scattered forests, sunny mountain slopes, one of the upper layer trees of stream valleys and lower seasonal rain forests at elevations of 500 - 1,400 metres.
Terminalia chebula: Scattered in teak forest, mixed deciduous forest, extending into forests of comparatively dry types; at elevations up to 1,500 metres, occasionally to 2,000 metres.
Thymus serpyllum: Dry stony ground, open sandy heaths and grassland in East Anglia.
Thymus vulgaris: Dry slopes, rocks and maquis. Always found on clay or limestone soils.
Tilia cordata: Woods on most fertile soils, especially limestone, it is commonly found on wooded limestone cliffs.
Tinospora cordifolia: Dry districts at low elevations. Deciduous and dry forests.
Tribulus terrestris: Dry open habitats, often as a weed in Europe. Sandy seashores in Japan.
Trifolium pratense: Meadows, pastures and other grassy places, especially on calcareous soils. Usually found on circumneutral soils.
Trigonella foenum-graecum: Field verges, uncultivated ground, dry grasslands and hillsides.
Tussilago farfara: Damp habitats, frequently on alkaline clays, in hedgebanks, roadsides, wasteland, often as a pioneer, and on dunes and shingle in coastal zones.
Ulmus rubra: Rich deep soils, often calcareous, on the banks of streams and low rocky hillsides.
Urtica dioica: Waste ground, hedgerows, woods etc, preferring a rich soil and avoiding acid soils.
Urtica urens: A weed of cultivated land and waste places, preferring light soils.
Vaccinium myrtillus: Heaths, moors and woods on acid soils to 1250 metres.
Valeriana officinalis: Grassland, scrub, woods etc, on dry or damp soils. Avoids acid soils.
Vanilla planifolia: An epiphytic plant, it grows wild in trees, producing aerial roots that penetrate fissures and cracks in the bark. Usually found climbing on trees in warm, wet tropical low land forests at elevations from sea-level to 600 metres.
Verbena officinalis: Waste ground and roadsides, avoiding acid soils and shady positions.
Viburnum opulus: Hedges, scrub and woodland, usually on damp soils.
Viola odorata: Fields, hedgerows and woodlands, especially on calcareous soils.
Viola tricolor: Cultivated and waste ground, short grassland etc, mainly on acid and neutral soils.
Viscum album: Grows on the branches of many trees, especially poplars, apples, chestnut and birch and especially on calcareous soils. Not usually found on conifers.
Vitex agnus-castus: Damp places by streams and on the littoral.
Vitis vinifera: Riversides and damp woods. Grows on the banks of the Thames at Kew in Britain.
Withania somnifera: Open places, disturbed areas etc. An undershrub in stony places.
Yucca elephantipes: Common in cultivation, or in hedges and thickets, throughout the lowlands and ascending commonly in the mountains to middle elevations; it is often seen at up to 2,700 metres or perhaps even higher.
Zingiber officinale: Not known in a truly wild situation.
Ziziphus jujuba: Dry gravelly or stony slopes of hills and mountains.
